prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Federal Data Terminations Tracker

The most policy-relevant, verified source of federal datasets terminated since January 2025.

Have a termination or removal to add? Contact us at removals@dataindex.us.

Read more about the methodology and why quantifying data terminations is so challenging in this Federation of American Scientists blogpost. To learn more about the Federal Data Terminations Tracker, watch our briefing.

Last updated: August 17, 2026.

Looking for the Dearly Departed Datasets tracker published in October 2025? View the archive →

Download CSV

Showing all 375 entries

Datasets Terminated 38

No entries in this section match your filters.

Disasters

Future Risk Index

Agency: FEMA

FEMA's interactive map projecting how much money climate-driven disasters would cost each U.S. county in the decades ahead.

Caveats: This is a model, not primary data, but it is an important product to come from the US Government instead of outside groups.

Sources

  • FEMA Removed Future Risk Index – Harvard Law School Environmental & Energy Law Program
  • The online climate tool that Trump removed, but data scientists have now rebuilt – Geographical (Royal Geographical Society)
  • fulton-ring/nri-future-risk – Fulton Ring (GitHub rebuild)
  • Archived copy (Wayback Machine)

Education

Program for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies, Cycle 2 (U.S. national files) (PIAAC)

Agency: ED

International assessment of adult literacy, numeracy, and problem solving; the U.S. fielded Cycle 2 in 2022-23 and published results, but the U.S. national data files were never released.

Caveats: OECD publishes an international dataset that includes U.S. cases, so the Cycle 2 data are not entirely unavailable. What was not released is the U.S. national public-use and restricted-use file, which NCES's own page promised by Spring 2025 and which historically carries variables unique to the United States — race and ethnicity and health among them — that the international file does not. Date terminated is left blank because the collection was completed rather than terminated; what is documented is a release that did not occur.

Sources

  • PIAAC Data Files – NCES program page
  • PIAAC Cycle 2 (2023) U.S. national results – NCES published product
  • PIAAC 2nd Cycle Database – OECD

Education

National Household Education Surveys Program 2023 (NHES:2023)

Agency: ED

NCES household survey of parents covering early childhood care and education, parent involvement in schooling, and homeschooling.

Caveats: Reports from the 2023 collection were published in September 2024; the data files were never released. NCES's own page continues to advertise a late-2024 release. Earlier NHES files remain available. Date terminated is left blank because the collection was completed rather than terminated — what is documented is a release that did not occur.

Sources

  • NHES Data Files and Questionnaires – NCES program page
  • National Household Education Surveys Program – NCES program page

Agriculture

Mink Survey

Agency: USDA

NASS's annual count of mink pelts produced and the farms producing them.

Sources

  • NASS Notice (August 28, 2025) – USDA NASS

Consumer finance

CFPB Consumer Complaint Narratives and Visualizations (CFPB)

Agency: CFPB

The free-text consumer complaint narratives and visualization tools published as part of CFPB's Consumer Complaint Database.

Caveats: The complaint database continues — CFPB is still collecting complaints, monitoring company responses, and sharing data with regulators. What ends is public publication of the free-text narratives and the visualization tools; previously published narratives move to CFPB's FOIA Reading Room, where they remain retrievable but not available in bulk. CFPB characterizes the publication as entirely discretionary. Date terminated reflects the agency's announcement.

Sources

  • The CFPB to Cease Discretionary Publication of Complaint Narratives and Visualizations – CFPB Newsroom

Labor

Employer Information Reports EEO-1 through EEO-6 (EEO-1)

Agency: EEOC

EEOC's mandatory workforce demographic reports covering private employers, state and local government, and public school systems.

Caveats: PROPOSED, NOT FINAL. The EEO-1 through EEO-6 filing, recordkeeping, and record-preservation requirements at 29 CFR part 1602 remain in force and covered employers remain obligated to comply. On July 23, 2026 the EEOC published a proposed rule that would rescind them; no final rule has been issued and the comment period closes August 24, 2026. The Commission may adopt, modify, or withdraw the proposal. Date terminated is left blank because no termination has taken effect. Rescinding the rule would not by itself discontinue the underlying information collection — OMB control number 3046-0049 should be tracked separately.

Sources

  • Removal of Reporting Requirements (proposed rule) – Federal Register Proposed Rule

Education

Progress in International Reading Literacy Study 2026 (U.S. participation) (PIRLS)

Agency: ED

International assessment of fourth-grade reading comprehension; the United States is absent from the 2026 cycle after participating in every round since 2001.

Caveats: The United States has participated in every PIRLS cycle since 2001 and does not appear on IEA's published participant list for 2026, which IEA gives as 64 education systems. The contract covering PIRLS, PIAAC, and PISA was terminated for convenience on February 12, 2025 and reinstated on March 6, 2025 in a modification titled for the international assessment program; no record reinstating the PIRLS scope has been located. NCES has issued no notice cancelling U.S. participation and we have received no statement from the Department — this entry records absence from the participant list, not an announced withdrawal. Date terminated reflects the reinstatement modification that excluded PIRLS. All prior PIRLS rounds remain available.

Sources

  • PIRLS 2026 participants – IEA
  • PIRLS Schedule and Plans – NCES program page

Education

Beginning Postsecondary Students, 2020 cohort second follow-up (BPS:20/25)

Agency: ED

Longitudinal study tracking first-time college students from entry through completion or departure; the planned 2025 second follow-up did not occur.

Caveats: The study is not fully terminated and earlier rounds remain available — the 2020/2022 data were released in DataLab in March 2026, and the contract remains active with modifications in March and June 2026. What ended is the 2025 second follow-up: the contract was terminated for convenience on February 10, 2025 and its total value cut by roughly $51 million while the NPSAS cross-sectional core was retained. Date terminated reflects that contract action. An RFI for NPSAS:28 includes optional BPS follow-up tasks, so a future cohort may begin.

Sources

  • Beginning Postsecondary Students Longitudinal Study – NCES program page
  • Contract 91990022C0017 modification history – FPDS-NG

Justice

National Law Enforcement Accountability Database (NLEAD)

Agency: DOJ

DOJ database of misconduct records for federal law enforcement officers, created so agencies could screen hires. Summary data published anually (only once in Dec 2025)

Sources

  • The National Law Enforcement Accountability Database – CRS Insight
  • National Law Enforcement Accountability Database – Bureau of Justice Statistics

Food security

Current Population Survey Food Security Supplement (CPS-FSS)

Agency: USDA

Annual survey supplement that measured how many American households struggled to afford enough food, the basis for USDA's yearly food insecurity report.

Sources

  • USDA Terminates Redundant Food Insecurity Survey – USDA Press Release
  • USDA’s Decision to End 30-Year Food Security Report Will Hide the Struggle of Millions of Families to Put Food on the Table – Source- Food Research & Action Center (FRAC)

Environment

Air Toxics Screening Assessment cancer risk estimates (AirToxScreen)

Agency: EPA

EPA's national screening estimates of cancer risk from hazardous air pollutants, published since 2

← Back to Tracker

Methodology

Last updated: December 2024

📁 Archive Notice: This tracker will be archived on December 31, 2025. Data collection will stop on that date and no further updates will be made.

Overview

This tracker collects federal job listing data from the official USAJobs APIs maintained by the U.S. Office of Personnel Management. Data is collected daily and stored in a public repository for transparency and reproducibility.

Repository: github.com/abigailhaddad/usajobs_historical

Data Sources

We collect from two complementary APIs:

Historical Jobs API

Endpoint: https://data.usajobs.gov/api/historicjoa
Documentation: developer.usajobs.gov/API-Reference/GET-api-historicjoa
Authentication: None required
What it returns: Job postings from the past (open or closed)
Our approach: Query one day at a time using StartPositionOpenDate and EndPositionOpenDate set to the same date
Code: scripts/collect_data.py

Current Jobs API

Endpoint: https://data.usajobs.gov/api/Search
Documentation: developer.usajobs.gov/API-Reference/GET-api-Search
Authentication: Requires API key (free from USAJobs)
What it returns: Jobs currently open for applications
Our approach: Query each occupational series separately (there are ~350) to work around the 10,000 result limit per query
Code: scripts/collect_current_data.py

Collection Schedule

Data is collected daily via GitHub Actions. Each run:

  1. Queries the historical API for the current day plus the previous 2 days (3-day overlap for redundancy)
  2. Queries the current API to capture all currently-open positions

The 3-day overlap ensures that if a job is missed on one day, it will be caught on subsequent runs. Combined with the current API as a backup, each job has multiple opportunities to be captured.

Code: update/update_all.py

Deduplication

Each job posting has a unique identifier (usajobsControlNumber). When we collect data:

  • New jobs are added to the dataset
  • Existing jobs are updated with the latest information
  • Jobs are never deleted from our historical record

Because both APIs capture the same jobs at different points in their lifecycle, there's built-in redundancy: if we miss a job from one API on a given day, we'll likely catch it from the other. Deduplication by control number ensures we don't double-count.

Appointment Types

Appointment type indicates whether a position is permanent, temporary, an internship, etc.

How We Get Appointment Types

The Current Jobs API returns numeric codes (e.g., 15328). We translate these to human-readable names by querying the official codelist:

Codelist endpoint: https://data.usajobs.gov/api/codelist/positionofferingtypes
Code: See fetch_position_offering_types() in scripts/collect_current_data.py

The Historical Jobs API returns appointment types as text strings directly.

Appointment Type Values

Code Name Description
15317 Permanent Ongoing position with no set end date
15318 Temporary Short-term position, usually under 1 year
15319 Term Time-limited position, typically 1-4 years
15322 Seasonal Recurring position tied to a particular season
15327 Multiple Posting includes multiple appointment types
15328 Internships Student internship positions
15326 Recent Graduates Pathways Recent Graduates program
15522 Intermittent Positions with irregular, as-needed schedules

To count internships: We filter for jobs where appointmentType equals "Internships" (or code 15328 in raw current API data).

Filling Data Gaps

Job postings include both an agency name (hiringAgencyName) and a department name (hiringDepartmentName), but occasionally one field is missing. When this happens:

  • Missing department: Look up from the agency name using a mapping built from the data
  • Missing agency name: Look up from the agency code

These mappings are generated automatically by analyzing which agency/department pairs appear together most frequently across all job postings.

Code: tracking/generate_agency_mappings.py

Data Storage

All data is stored in Apache Parquet format, grouped by year based on positionOpenDate. The complete dataset is available in the repository under data/.

Reproducing This Analysis

# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/abigailhaddad/usajobs_historical

# Install dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt

# See README for collection script details
# Summary generation:
python tracking/generate_jobs_summary_dynamic.py

Contact

Questions about methodology? Open an issue on GitHub.

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: National Survey of Children's Health (NSCH)
Description: The National Survey of Children's Health is a household survey that produces national and state-level data on the physical and emotional health of children 0 - 17 years old in the United States. The survey collects information related to the health and well-being of children, including access to and use of health care, family interactions, parental health, school and after-school experiences, and neighborhood characteristics.
URL: https://census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch.html

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# National Survey of Children’s Health (NSCH): Research and Preservation Report

**Research snapshot:** October 9, 2026.  
**Principal finding:** Your title, description, and URL are accurate. The NSCH is best understood as an ongoing federal statistical program with annual datasets—not a single, unchanging data file.

**Most important cautions:** Do not directly compare the pre-2016 and redesigned surveys; use the revised weights for historical annual files; account for the complex sample design and income imputation; and preserve documentation and release versions alongside the data.

## 1. Dataset identity and verification

| Attribute | Verified information |
|---|---|
| Official title | National Survey of Children’s Health |
| Acronym | NSCH |
| Canonical program URL | https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch.html |
| Federal sponsor and program lead | Maternal and Child Health Bureau (MCHB), Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) |
| Current survey operator and public-use file producer | U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Department of Commerce |
| Type | Sample household survey; repeated cross-sectional data |
| Principal population | Children ages 0–17 living in households |
| Principal geographic coverage | United States: 50 states and District of Columbia |
| Principal estimation levels | National and state |
| Frequency | Annual since the 2016 redesign |
| Latest release located | **2025 survey data, released October 2026** |
| Principal access products | Downloadable public-use microdata, documentation, and interactive indicator tools |

Your description closely matches Census’s official description. It correctly identifies physical and emotional health, health-care access and use, family interactions, parental health, school and after-school experiences, and neighborhood characteristics.

Two additions make it more complete:

* The survey includes **mental, behavioral, and developmental health** and many social and family circumstances related to health.
* It explicitly measures the **prevalence and impact of children with special health care needs (CSHCN)**, including insurance adequacy, medical homes, service access, and care coordination.

The target population should not be interpreted as literally every U.S. child: the household-based design does not provide equivalent coverage of institutionalized children, children outside housing units, or U.S. territories. [Census overview](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch.html); [2025 methodology](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch/technical-documentation/methodology/2025-NSCH-Methodology-Report.pdf)

## 2. Who funds, conducts, publishes, and distributes it?

These roles are divided among several organizations.

### HRSA MCHB: sponsor and substantive steward

HRSA says it **funds and directs** the NSCH. MCHB establishes its child-health policy and measurement purposes and supports its use in maternal and child health programs.

Additional agencies and state partners may sponsor particular content or larger samples. This means the survey has a stable federal core but can evolve through partner-funded enhancements.

### Census Bureau: survey operation and official microdata

Census conducts the survey on behalf of HHS. Its responsibilities include sampling, questionnaire administration, processing, weighting, confidentiality protection, and producing final public-use datasets and technical documentation.

The Census website is the principal source for the official post-2016 microdata releases.

### CDC/NCHS: historical survey custodian

Before the redesign, the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), within CDC, conducted NSCH through the State and Local Area Integrated Telephone Survey—**SLAITS**. CDC maintains historical survey resources and restricted-data information for that era.

### CAHMI/Data Resource Center: access, derived indicators, and assistance

The **Child and Adolescent Health Measurement Initiative (CAHMI)** operates the **Data Resource Center for Child & Adolescent Health (DRC)**. It provides interactive queries, state comparisons, maps, constructed indicators, enhanced datasets, codebooks, and technical assistance.

**Census microdata and DRC constructed datasets are related but not interchangeable.** DRC products contain additional derived variables and may have different update schedules or weight versions. Their provenance must be recorded separately.

Sources: [HRSA program overview](https://mchb.hrsa.gov/data-research/national-survey-childrens-health); [HRSA participant FAQ](https://mchb.hrsa.gov/data-research/national-survey-childrens-health/participants-frequently-asked-questions); [DRC FAQ](https://www.childhealthdata.org/about-us/faq)

## 3. Legal authority, mandate, and confidentiality

### Core authorities

The principal legal authorities documented for the survey are:

| Authority | Role |
|---|---|
| **13 U.S.C. § 8(b)** | Allows Census to conduct surveys on behalf of other agencies. |
| **Social Security Act § 501(a)(2), 42 U.S.C. § 701(a)(2)** | Provides the maternal and child health authority cited for HHS’s collection of this information. |
| **13 U.S.C. § 9** | Protects confidential survey responses. |
| **13 U.S.C. § 23(c)** | Supports access by authorized individuals with Census Special Sworn Status. |
| **OMB control number 0607-0990** | Identifies the collection under the Paperwork Reduction Act clearance process. |

Some collection notices also cite **42 U.S.C. § 241** and **42 U.S.C. § 1769d(a)(4)(B)** in connection with additional sponsoring authorities. Those citations should be interpreted in the context of the relevant collection year and sponsor, rather than treated as the sole basis for every NSCH release.

### “Authorized” does not mean participation is mandatory

**Household participation is voluntary.** The survey’s authorizing statutes, program responsibilities, and OMB clearance should not be confused with a requirement that sampled families respond.

Nor should NSCH be described without qualification as a statute-mandated annual census of children. It is an authorized statistical survey serving federal and state program needs.

### Public participation in survey governance

The Paperwork Reduction Act process generates Federal Register notices and opportunities to comment on necessity, burden, methodology, and collection design. OMB supporting statements and questionnaire appendices are valuable records for understanding why questions or procedures changed.

Sources: [Federal Register collection notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2019/11/19/2019-24962/proposed-information-collection-comment-request-national-survey-of-childrens-health); [2025 data-user FAQ](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch/technical-documentation/methodology/2025-NSCH-FAQs.pdf); [2026 collection-record mirror](https://omb.report/icr/202603-0607-004)

## 4. History and major breaks in the series

| Period | Development | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| **2001** | First National Survey of Children with Special Health Care Needs (NS-CSHCN). | Important predecessor, but a distinct survey. |
| **2003** | First NSCH; fieldwork extended into 2004. | Beginning of the broad child-health survey series. |
| **2007** | Second NSCH; fieldwork extended into 2008. | Historical telephone-survey wave. |
| **2011–2012** | Third pre-redesign NSCH. | Last principal NSCH wave before redesign. |
| **2015** | Redesigned survey pretested. | Transition to new instruments and collection design. |
| **2016** | NSCH and NS-CSHCN content integrated into one redesigned survey, operated by Census using address-based sampling. Annual collection began. | **Major comparability break.** |
| **2022 onward** | Race/ethnicity-related imputation and weighting enhancements introduced; corresponding changes applied retroactively to 2016–2021 microdata. | Historical release version becomes essential. |
| **2025 survey / 2026 release** | Latest release located; fieldwork extended because of a lapse in federal appropriations. No screener public-use file released for this year. | Preserve the changed release structure and actual collection dates. |

### Why 2016 is a hard boundary

The original surveys used telephone sampling and interviews through NCHS/SLAITS. The redesigned survey changed the sampling frame, collection modes, and questionnaire content.

Official guidance says **trends or comparisons between pre-2016 and redesigned NSCH estimates should not be made**. An observed difference could reflect methodological change rather than a change in children’s health.

### A second, subtler boundary: revised historical weights

Census re-released historical files with enhanced weighting. The documented naming convention includes:

* `nsch_YYYYe_topical`
* `nsch_YYYYe_screener`, where applicable

The DRC warns that archived estimates based on the original 2016–2021 weights should not be compared directly with newer estimates based on revised weights. Recalculating historical estimates from the revised files is preferable to mixing old tables with new results.

## 5. What information does it contain?

Content varies by year and child age. Broad domains include:

| Domain | Examples |
|---|---|
| Child characteristics | Age, sex, race, Hispanic origin, language, special health care needs |
| Physical, mental, and developmental health | Reported diagnoses, current conditions, functional difficulties |
| Insurance | Coverage, type, continuity, adequacy |
| Health services | Preventive visits, dental care, specialty services, unmet need |
| Care quality and coordination | Medical home, shared decision-making, coordinated care |
| Early childhood | Birth-related information, infant feeding, developmental and school-readiness measures |
| School and activities | School experiences, engagement, after-school activities, age-appropriate behaviors |
| Family circumstances | Income relative to poverty, parental health, family interactions, housing and nutrition |
| Impact on families | Time, financial, caregiving, and employment consequences of a child’s health needs |
| Neighborhood | Safety, support, amenities, and neighborhood conditions |
| Adolescent transition | Preparation for adult health care and related services |

### Age-specific instruments

There are three topical questionnaires:

* **T1:** ages 0–5
* **T2:** ages 6–11
* **T3:** ages 12–17

A variable absent for some children may therefore be **outside their questionnaire universe**, not a missing response.

### Content changes matter

For example, the 2025 FAQ documents additions concerning asthma attacks, age at first reported fetal alcohol spectrum disorder diagnosis, nonparental care hours, and ADHD medication shortages. It also documents removals of outdoor-play questions and expansion of fruit/vegetable items to older children.

For any longitudinal indicator, check exact wording, age eligibility, response categories, recall period, and construction rules—not merely the variable name.

Source: [2025 FAQ](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch/technical-documentation/methodology/2025-NSCH-FAQs.pdf)

## 6. How the survey is collected

### Basic workflow

1. Census selects residential addresses.
2. A **household screener** identifies children, collects roster information, and assesses special health care needs.
3. **One child is selected** from each eligible household using the documented selection probabilities.
4. An adult familiar with that child’s health and health care completes the appropriate topical questionnaire.
5. Census processes, imputes selected variables, weights, and disclosure-reviews the data.

The topical record is principally a **selected-child record**, not a clinical encounter, insurance claim, school record, or complete sibling history.

The annual NSCH is **repeated cross-sectional**, not a panel following the same children annually.

### Modes and languages

The redesigned survey uses mailed invitations and online or paper questionnaires. Telephone assistance can also administer the web questionnaire. Instruments are available in **English and Spanish**.

The adult respondent reports information about the child; this is not principally a direct child interview or medical examination.

### Sampling design

For 2025, the frame came from Census’s **Master Address File**, supplemented with administrative-record and geographic information indicating likely child presence.

Addresses were classified into three frame strata. Sampling occurred in the two strata expected to cover approximately 95% of households with children in each state; the lowest-probability stratum was excluded.

The design also gives differential selection probabilities to children with special health care needs and young children. Some states purchase additional samples. Consequently, **raw sample percentages are not population estimates**.

### Latest-wave operational facts

| 2025 survey measure | Value |
|---|---:|
| Sampled addresses | Approximately 360,000 |
| Completed screeners | Approximately 108,000 |
| Screeners with eligible children | Approximately 56,000 |
| Complete or sufficiently complete topical interviews | **45,139** |
| Weighted overall response rate | **34.7%** |
| Weighted interview completion rate | **77.1%** |
| Topical responses through web instrument | **88.6%** |
| Topical responses on paper | **11.4%** |
| Collection period | **June 20, 2025–March 6, 2026** |

The two response rates have different denominators: the interview completion rate concerns households that initiate the process; the overall rate also incorporates address resolution.

Twelve states funded 2025 oversamples: Arizona, California, Colorado, Illinois, Kansas, Nebraska, New Mexico, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Utah, West Virginia, and Wyoming.

Fieldwork was extended following the October–November 2025 appropriations lapse and pause in operations. Thus, “2025” identifies the survey cycle, **not an assurance that every interview occurred in calendar 2025**.

## 8. What data scientists need to know

### Survey weights and variance estimation

For topical analysis, the final child weight is **`FWC`**.

The documented design variables include:

* **`FIPSST`** — state
* **`STRATUM`** — sampling stratum
* **`HHID`** — household identifier used as the primary sampling unit

Where software accepts only one stratum identifier, Census recommends crossing state and sampling stratum.

Use survey-aware estimation for percentages, totals, regressions, standard errors, and confidence intervals. Treating the records as an ordinary simple random sample can produce misleading uncertainty.

For subgroup analysis, use **domain/subpopulation procedures** rather than deleting all other records. The FAQ identifies state-only subsetting as an exception that does not compromise variance estimation.

### Income and other imputation

Selected demographic variables are imputed for weighting. The public files contain imputation flags.

Poverty ratio has **six implicates**, documented as `FPL_I1` through `FPL_I6`. Analyses involving income/poverty should follow the multiple-imputation guide and combine estimates and uncertainty appropriately. Choosing one implicate understates the information needed to account for imputation uncertainty.

Most health-item nonresponse should not be assumed to have been imputed simply because selected demographic variables were.

### Combining years

Census permits combining compatible post-redesign years to improve precision. Its guidance says to divide each annual weight by the number of years combined when estimating an average annual or midpoint population.

Also:

* Use consistently revised releases.
* Harmonize stratum coding, particularly `2a` versus `2`.
* Follow the multi-year guide for design identifiers.
* Check question changes and age universes.
* Identify pooled estimates as multi-year estimates, not a single-year result.
* Remember that overlapping pooled periods share observations.

### Missing values and disclosure suppression

Preserve distinctions among valid responses, item nonresponse, structural skips, and confidentiality suppression. The methodology identifies **`.D`** as “suppressed for confidentiality” for certain geographic variables.

When converting SAS/Stata files to CSV or another format, explicitly preserve special missing-value semantics, labels, identifier strings, and response codes.

### Geography and linkage

The 2025 public-use geography variables include:

* `FIPSST`
* `CBSAFP_YN`
* `METRO_YN`
* `MPC_YN`

These last three describe geographic status, **not named counties or cities**. Some values are suppressed to prevent identification of small areas.

State-level contextual joins can support analysis, but person-level linkage to identifiable external records is prohibited under the published conditions.

Source: [2025 FAQ](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch/technical-documentation/methodology/2025-NSCH-FAQs.pdf); [2025 methodology](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch/technical-documentation/methodology/2025-NSCH-Methodology-Report.pdf)

## 9. Typical users and public benefits

### Documented users

HRSA identifies families, communities, policymakers, child advocates, educators, researchers, and the public. Particularly important users are:

* State **Title V Maternal and Child Health** programs
* Federal maternal and child health officials
* Public-health analysts and epidemiologists
* Pediatric and health-services researchers
* Disability and special-health-care-needs organizations
* Education and early-childhood program leaders
* Legislative staff, journalists, and policy advocates

### Concrete public purposes

**Program accountability.** HRSA reports that NSCH supplies data for **29 Title V national outcome and performance measures**.

**Needs assessment.** Results support states’ five-year Title V needs assessments and help identify unmet service needs.

**National objectives.** HRSA’s participant FAQ identifies contributions to **15 Healthy People 2030 child-health objectives**.

**Visibility beyond administrative records.** Claims and clinical records describe people who reach particular services. NSCH also captures unmet needs, insurance adequacy, family burden, neighborhood conditions, and children without a recorded encounter in a particular system.

**Equity analysis.** Researchers can investigate differences by income, race/ethnicity, age, special health care needs, and other characteristics, subject to sample-size and measurement limitations.

**Public access.** Free files and interactive tools make evidence available outside government and large research institutions.

These are demonstrated uses and capacities, not proof that the survey itself causes better health outcomes or automatically determines funding allocations.

Sources: [HRSA overview](https://mchb.hrsa.gov/data-research/national-survey-childrens-health); [participant FAQ](https://mchb.hrsa.gov/data-research/national-survey-childrens-health/participants-frequently-asked-questions)

## 10. Limitations and responsible policy interpretation

1. **Parent/caregiver reporting.** Diagnoses, service experiences, and family circumstances reflect respondent knowledge and recall, not independent clinical verification.
2. **Diagnosis is partly an access measure.** Reported diagnosed prevalence can vary with screening, service access, and recognition of conditions.
3. **Nonresponse remains consequential.** Weighting mitigates differences but does not guarantee elimination of bias.
4. **Household coverage is incomplete.** Institutionalized children and children outside ordinary housing units are not equivalently represented; territories require separate resources.
5. **Language coverage matters.** English and Spanish instruments do not eliminate barriers affecting other-language households.
6. **Small subgroups may be imprecise.** State samples do not support every rare condition or finely divided demographic group.
7. **Local estimates require special care.** Restricted geography does not by itself make the sample representative of every county or ZIP code.
8. **Cross-sectional associations are not causal effects.**
9. **Recall periods vary.** “Ever,” “current,” and “past 12 months” measures answer different questions.
10. **Rankings can exaggerate differences.** State league tables should show confidence intervals and recognize sampling error and multiple comparisons.

For advocacy, a defensible presentation states the survey year or pooled period, release version, population, indicator definition, weighted estimate, and uncertainty.

## 11. Privacy, reuse, and ethical requirements

The public files are disclosure-reviewed statistical products, not identifiable household records.

Published requirements instruct users to:

* Use the files for statistical reporting and analysis only.
* Make no use of an identity discovered inadvertently or otherwise.
* Not link them to individually identifiable Census or non-Census records.

Federal-government works generally receive public-domain treatment under U.S. copyright law, but **copyright status is not permission to disregard confidentiality or data-use restrictions**. DRC-derived materials may also carry their own agreement or attribution conditions.

Sensitive subjects—including child mental health, disability, household hardship, and family circumstances—also warrant care in subgroup reporting. Avoid stigmatizing interpretations or unsupported explanations for disparities.

Source: [2025 data-use conditions](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch/technical-documentation/methodology/2025-NSCH-FAQs.pdf)

## 12. Preservation and library recommendations

### Minimum preservation package

Preserve each release as a complete, versioned package:

| Component | Reason |
|---|---|
| Original SAS/Stata files and associated inputs/formats | Authoritative values, labels, types, and missing codes |
| Open-format derivatives plus schema | Long-term accessibility without losing semantics |
| Questionnaires, English and Spanish | Exact wording, routing, and age universes |
| Variable lists/codebooks | Interpretation |
| Frequencies | Validation and baseline checks |
| Methodology and source/accuracy reports | Sampling, response, weighting, and limitations |
| FAQs and analytic guides | Operational rules for correct use |
| Imputation and pooling instructions | Reproducibility |
| Release notes and weighting-enhancement documents | Version and comparability history |
| DRC construction code and indicator definitions | Derived-measure provenance |
| Federal Register and OMB records | Authority, burden, and design history |
| Landing-page snapshots and download manifest | Evidence of what was available when |

### Record metadata at file level

At minimum record:

* Survey cycle and actual fieldwork dates
* Publication date and retrieval date
* Sponsor, creator, distributor, and derivative producer
* Original URL and filename
* Release/weight version
* Record count and file format
* Geographic and age coverage
* Rights and statistical-use conditions
* Dependencies on formats, code, and documentation
* Cryptographic checksum
* Relationship to superseded files and related products

### Preserve superseded releases without silently replacing them

Old releases may be necessary to reproduce published findings. Retain them, but clearly mark them **superseded** and document the revised-weight replacements.

Do not overwrite a historical file solely because the basename is reused. Similarly, archive interactive tables with their query parameters, denominator, definition, uncertainty, and weight version.

### Current preservation risks

* **Version ambiguity:** revised weights can change estimates without changing the nominal survey year.
* **Distributed stewardship:** Census, HRSA, CDC, and DRC hold different pieces of the record.
* **Changing release structure:** the 2025 screener-file omission must be documented.
* **Proprietary formats:** conversion can lose labels and special missing values.
* **Mutable interactive products:** historical queries may cease to reproduce earlier results.
* **Funding and operations disruptions:** the 2025 fieldwork interruption illustrates dependence on appropriations.
* **Stale landing pages:** at this research snapshot, Census documented the 2025 release while HRSA’s general overview still called 2024 the newest dataset.

The last point is especially important: **verify the release-specific page and documentation, not only the program homepage.**

[Format and release/version]. Retrieved [date] from https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch/data/datasets.html.

### Matters not established by the reviewed sources

I did not verify:

* A dataset-wide DOI

## Bottom line

NSCH is a major public resource for understanding children’s health **together with the family, service, school, and neighborhood contexts in which health develops**. Its state-level design and standardized measures make it particularly valuable for public-health accountability and advocacy.

For preservation and reuse, the essential unit is **the versioned data-and-documentation package**. A microdata file alone cannot reliably establish which population it represents, how uncertainty should be calculated, or whether its estimates are comparable with another year.

# NSCH Dataset Risk Assessment

**Assessment date: October 9, 2026**  
**Dataset:** National Survey of Children’s Health (NSCH)  
**Primary publisher:** U.S. Census Bureau, on behalf of HRSA’s Maternal and Child Health Bureau (MCHB).

## Overall finding

**The strongest evidence points to selective loss of information and reduced public-use detail, rather than imminent termination of the entire survey.** NSCH continues to publish data and has active OMB clearance. Nevertheless, there are documented operational interruptions, a discontinued public-use product, substantial agency staffing losses, and reports of politically sensitive information being removed.

Additional research also uncovered an important omission from my earlier report: **data users reported in April 2025 that responses to `ACE12`—a question about unfair treatment because of sexual orientation or gender identity—had been replaced with missing values.** This warrants a more cautious historical-availability assessment.

These ratings apply to the **NSCH program and its public-use products**, not just whether its homepage loads. They are rubric classifications, not numerical probabilities of disappearance. I distinguish confirmed agency actions, reported observations, and proposals below.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

- **Gone — Not supported.** Historical release pages remain available. Census lists screener and topical files for, among others, [2016](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch/data/datasets/nsch2016.html), [2017](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch/data/datasets/nsch2017.html), and [2024](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch/data/datasets/nsch2024.html).
- **High Risk — Not established.** I did not establish that entire historical annual data files have been removed. The discontinuation of the **2025** screener product concerns a new cycle, not demonstrated removal of earlier screener files.
- **Moderate Risk — Supported by reported element-level alteration.** In the Population Reference Bureau’s Federal Data Forum, Beth Jarosz reported on April 14, 2025, that `ACE12` had been removed. On April 25, she clarified that the variable remained in the file but its values had been converted to missing. That is directly relevant to the rubric’s element-removal threshold. [Data-user discussion](https://federaldataforum.prb.org/acsdatausersgroup/discussion/national-survey-of-childrens-health-altered)
- **No Known Issue — Supported for broad file availability, but not for unchanged contents.** Historical files remain listed, and Census documents legitimate retrospective weighting revisions. However, continued file availability does not negate the reported `ACE12` alteration.

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk**

The reported replacement of substantive responses with missing values is an element-level loss, even if filenames and variable names survive.

**Confidence: moderate.** The specific observation comes from an identifiable data expert and is echoed in concerns submitted during the 2026 clearance process. I did **not** perform a before-and-after binary comparison or establish exactly which historical releases were affected. Consequently, this rating should be treated as provisional pending a file-level audit.

**Preservation implication:** Archive existing historical files immediately, but do not assume a newly downloaded file is identical to its earlier release.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

- **Gone — Not supported.** Census released the 2025 topical data in October 2026; the survey has not been terminated. [2025 FAQ](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch/technical-documentation/methodology/2025-NSCH-FAQs.pdf)
- **High Risk — Not supported for the overall survey.** I found no established skipped annual survey cycle, missed statutory publication deadline, or ICR expiration exceeding one year.
- **Moderate Risk — Directly supported.** Census states that 2025 collection was extended because the October–November 2025 lapse in appropriations paused survey operations. Collection ran from June 2025 through March 2026. This satisfies the rubric’s **collection-delayed** condition. [2025 FAQ](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch/technical-documentation/methodology/2025-NSCH-FAQs.pdf)
- **No Known Issue — Strong countervailing evidence.** OMB’s indexed record for ICR **202603-0607-004** shows approval with change on **June 16, 2026**, active status, and expiration on **June 30, 2029**. Federal Register notices describe continued annual collection. [OMB record](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202603-0607-004); [March 2026 notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/03/25/2026-05796/agency-information-collection-activities-submission-to-the-office-of-management-and-budget-omb-for)

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk**

The collection interruption is documented, although collection and publication subsequently resumed. Active clearance substantially lowers the immediate risk of total termination.

This is a rating of **recent demonstrated disruption**, not a claim that the next release is already overdue. OMB approval permits collection; it does not guarantee funding or future publication.

## 3. Data Quality

### Evidence by risk level

- **Gone — Not supported.** Collection and publication continue.
- **High Risk — Directly supported by reduced public-use detail.** Census discontinued the **stand-alone Screener Public Use File beginning with the 2025 survey**. Earlier screeners included all rostered children in completed screener households; the topical file includes selected-child and household information for households completing the topical interview. Thus, the topical product is not a complete replacement for the screener product. Census attributes the change to confidentiality protection and evolving disclosure risks. [2025 methodology report](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch/technical-documentation/methodology/2025-NSCH-Methodology-Report.pdf)
- **Moderate Risk — Also supported.** Operational pauses, staffing losses, and uncertain documentation of sensitive-variable changes create additional risks to timeliness and reproducibility.
- **No Known Issue — Supported for some dimensions.** The proposed 2026 sample increases from approximately **360,000 to 400,000 addresses**, with continued state oversampling and response-improvement measures. Those changes could improve precision. [December 2025 Federal Register notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/12/05/2025-22134/agency-information-collection-activities-submission-to-the-office-of-management-and-budget-omb-for)

### Selected level: **High Risk**

The loss of the screener public-use product is an **actual reduction in publicly available analytical detail**, meeting the high-risk threshold independently of the reported `ACE12` issue.

This does **not** mean remaining topical estimates are generally inaccurate. Confidentiality protection can be justified while still reducing research access and longitudinal analytical capability.

## 4. Statutory Context

### Evidence by risk level

- **Gone — Not applicable** under this category.
- **High Risk — Not the best fit.** NSCH has identified legal authorities and substantial programmatic uses. It is not an unsupported collection with no demonstrated users.
- **Moderate Risk — Supported.** The cited authorities authorize Census’s work for other agencies and HHS maternal and child health information collection, but I did not identify a statute specifically requiring an **annual NSCH public-use release with protected question content**. Its continuity depends partly on administrative implementation and funding choices.
- **No Known Issue — Meaningful countervailing evidence.** NSCH supports Title V maternal and child health needs assessment and performance measurement. HRSA identifies it as a source for **29 Title V national outcome and performance measures**. The documented authorities include **13 U.S.C. §8(b)** and **42 U.S.C. §701(a)(2)**. [Authority notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2019/11/19/2019-24962/proposed-information-collection-comment-request-national-survey-of-childrens-health); [HRSA program overview](https://mchb.hrsa.gov/data-research/national-survey-childrens-health)

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk**

NSCH is strongly embedded in program implementation, but its particular annual collection, publication products, and individual questions are not clearly locked into statute.

Other surveys and administrative records cover parts of children’s health. I found no equivalent substitute combining NSCH’s state-level design, special-health-care-needs measures, and family/service context.

**Rubric ambiguity:** Because “required for implementation of a federal program” also appears in your *No Known Issue* definition, that rating could be defensible under a broad interpretation. I select **Moderate Risk** because program dependence provides less protection against question removal or product discontinuation than a specific statutory collection/publication mandate.

## 5. Staffing and Funding

### Evidence by risk level

- **Gone — Not supported.** Neither all relevant staff nor all survey funding have disappeared; current releases and renewed clearance demonstrate continued operation.
- **High Risk — Supported at the operating-agency level.** In May 2025, acting Census Director Ron Jarmin reportedly said Census had lost **more than 1,000 employees** through early retirement and voluntary separation. - **Moderate Risk — Supported at the sponsoring agency/bureau level.** KFF Health News estimated that HRSA lost **more than 700 workers—approximately one-quarter of its workforce—between February and June 2025**. Former MCHB leader Michael Warren described bureau cuts as substantial. An April 2025 Senate letter reported **20% staffing cuts at MCHB**. These are reported estimates, not audited NSCH-team counts. [KFF investigation](https://kffhealthnews.org/health-industry/hrsa-federal-staff-cuts-affect-health-programs-grants/); [Senate letter](https://www.gillibrand.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/250416_Letter-re-HRSA-Cuts-to-Primary-Care-and-Maternal-Health-Workforce_FINAL.pdf)
- **No Known Issue — Not supported agency-wide.** Continued survey work is reassuring, but it does not demonstrate losses below the rubric’s thresholds.

### Selected level: **High Risk**

Census’s reported loss of over 1,000 employees meets the rubric explicitly. HRSA/MCHB losses add sponsor-side vulnerability. July 2026 reporting continued to describe statistical agencies as strained and Census as operating under acting leadership. [Government Executive](https://www.govexec.com/workforce/2026/07/staffing-cuts-are-leaving-federal-statistical-agencies-stretched-thin/415104/)

**Important qualifications:**

- These are **agency/bureau-level exposures**, not a finding that the NSCH team itself lost 1,000 people.
- The FY2026 proposal to eliminate HRSA as a separate organizational entity is a **proposal**, not proof that NSCH funding was eliminated. KFF reports both the proposal and HHS’s stated intention to maintain essential services.
- I did not establish an enacted **20% NSCH-specific budget cut**.
- Temporary shutdown furloughs should not be counted as permanent staff losses.

## 6. Policy

### Evidence by risk level

- **Gone — Not supported.** The survey continues.
- **High Risk — Supported by reported implemented changes and corroborating policy research.** The `ACE12` alteration was reported as already implemented, not merely proposed. A February 2026 Williams Institute report includes NSCH among federal collections affected by removal of sexual-orientation/gender-identity-related measures. San José State University’s library guide also identifies **NSCH 2025** among collections affected by presidential-action changes associated with **Executive Order 14168**. [Data-user report](https://federaldataforum.prb.org/acsdatausersgroup/discussion/national-survey-of-childrens-health-altered); [Williams Institute report](https://williamsinstitute.law.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/Federal-SOGI-Data-Collection-Feb-2026.pdf); [SJSU guide](https://library.sjsu.edu/c.php?g=230129&p=9551432)
- **Moderate Risk — Independently supported.** Executive Order **14212**, establishing the Make America Healthy Again Commission, explicitly directs evaluation of NSCH’s effectiveness as a childhood-health data source. That review alone does not mandate removal, but places survey content and methods under administration-directed scrutiny. [Executive order, §5(a)(viii)](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/02/19/2025-02871/establishing-the-presidents-make-america-healthy-again-commission)
- **No Known Issue — Not supported.** Evidence of post-January 2025 changes and stakeholder concerns prevents this classification.

### Selected level: **High Risk**

Implemented removal of sensitive information, as reported by data users and corroborated by broader policy research, is more serious than a pending proposal.

**Confidence: moderate.** I could not inspect the complete underlying presidential-action ICR amendment directly during this review. The attribution to EO14168 relies on secondary documentation. Public comments in the 2026 ICR package also raise concerns about `ACE12`, but comments are evidence of stakeholder concerns—not, by themselves, proof of agency action. [Public comments](https://omb.report/icr/202603-0607-004/doc/original/167213600.pdf)

## Practical preservation priorities

1. **Preserve annual microdata and documentation together**, including historical screener files and superseded releases.
2. **Audit `ACE12` values across versions**, not just whether the variable exists. Record affected years, missing-value codes, and changes in nonmissing counts.
3. **Record checksums and retrieval dates.** A working URL is not evidence of unchanged contents.
4. **Preserve independent copies where lawfully available**, including DRC constructed data and indicator definitions; do not assume they are complete or byte-identical backups.
5. **Monitor OMB 0607-0990, Federal Register notices, and release schedules**, alongside funding and staffing developments.

There is insufficient evidence to assign a numerical probability that NSCH will disappear entirely. The immediate preservation concern is narrower but significant: **accessible files may no longer contain all previously available information, and future products may provide less detail.**
